title: Nothing in Myself, Held by Christ

sections.heading: Coming to you as a creature remade by grace
sections.text:
Lord, I come to you as someone very small: a body made from dust, held together only because you give me life. Yet you have also given me an unseen soul, and by your hidden grace you have made me new.

I am not impressive. I bring no treasure of my own. In myself I have nothing to boast about. Still, you chose me before I ever came looking for you, gave me to Christ, and brought me to life again by your Spirit. That mercy is the only reason I can come to you at all.
theological_themes: Human frailty and creatureliness before God
Regeneration as the unseen work of grace
Election and belonging to Christ as mercy, not personal merit

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds the prayer’s picture of human life as both earthy and God-given: humanity is formed from dust and lives only because God gives breath.
Paul speaks of God choosing and adopting his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, supporting the prayer’s confession that salvation begins in God’s gracious initiative.
Jesus describes new birth as the work of the Spirit, unseen and sovereign, which matches the prayer’s language of being made new by an invisible power of grace.

sections.heading: Seeing the emptiness of sin and the fullness of Christ
sections.text:
Father, I am becoming more deeply aware of what sin really is—how evil it is, how miserable it makes me, and how empty it leaves me. I see more clearly that created things cannot carry the weight I put on them.

But I also see this: Christ is enough. What I cannot repair, he can restore. What I cannot fill, he can satisfy. What I cannot cleanse, he can make clean.
theological_themes: Sin as both guilt and misery
Created things are good but cannot be ultimate
Christ’s sufficiency for cleansing, restoration, and satisfaction

scripture_references.connection: God exposes the folly of forsaking him for broken cisterns, which supports the prayer’s contrast between the vanity of created things and the life found in God.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers are filled in him, grounding the prayer’s confidence that Christ is sufficient.

sections.heading: Confessing how I try to take your place
sections.text:
When you want to guide me, I grab the steering wheel. When you call me to trust your rule, I try to run my own life. When you offer to care for me, I act as if I am enough for myself.

When I should depend on what you provide, I scramble to secure everything on my own. When I should receive your providence, I insist on my own way. When I should give myself to knowing you, loving you, honoring you, and trusting you, I end up serving myself.

I even try to edit your commands so they fit what I already want. I look for people’s approval more than yours. Left to myself, I do not simply make mistakes—I make idols.
theological_themes: Self-rule as rebellion against God’s lordship
Idolatry shown in craving approval and reshaping God’s commands

scripture_references.connection: This passage calls God’s people to trust him rather than lean on their own understanding, directly addressing the prayer’s confession of self-direction and self-reliance.
Paul describes the human exchange of God’s glory for created things, which gives biblical weight to the prayer’s diagnosis of the heart as naturally idolatrous.
Paul contrasts seeking human approval with serving Christ, illuminating the prayer’s confession that the desire for people’s praise can displace loyalty to God.

sections.heading: Asking you to bring my heart back
sections.text:
Lord, my deepest need is for my heart to come back to you.

Convince me, not just in theory but down inside, that I cannot be my own god. I cannot make myself happy. I cannot be my own savior and recover my joy by my own strength. I cannot be my own Holy Spirit, teaching myself, guiding myself, and ruling myself.

Bring me back to depending on you completely.
theological_themes: Repentance as the heart returning to God
Dependence on Christ for restoration and on the Spirit for guidance and rule

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing, supporting the prayer’s rejection of self-sufficiency in spiritual life and fruitfulness.
David asks God for a clean heart, renewed spirit, restored joy, and sustaining grace, which closely matches the prayer’s desire for God to restore and rule the inner life.
Paul presents life and holiness as dependent on the Spirit’s work, not self-rule, supporting the prayer’s admission that only the Spirit can lead and govern rightly.

sections.heading: Receiving your hard mercies when you strip away my idols
sections.text:
Teach me to recognize your grace even when it comes through painful providence.

When my reputation starts to feel secure, you know how to humble me. When money becomes my idol, you can make it fly away. When pleasure becomes everything to me, you can turn it bitter so I stop drinking poison and calling it life.

Do not let me waste your discipline. Use even the hard things to loosen my grip on false gods and bring me nearer to you.
theological_themes: God’s providence over humbling and loss
Affliction as fatherly discipline for holiness
Grace that exposes and removes idols

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews interprets God’s discipline as the loving correction of a Father who aims at holiness and peace, which supports the prayer’s request to see affliction as purposeful grace.
The psalmist testifies that affliction corrected his wandering and led him back to God’s word, fitting the prayer’s plea that hardship would bring the heart back to God.

sections.heading: Bringing me to the cross and keeping me there
sections.text:
Take away my restless eyes, my curiosity that feeds sin, my greedy appetite, and my lustful heart. Show me that none of these things can heal a guilty conscience, steady a collapsing body, or carry my soul when I come to the end of my life.

Then bring me to the cross of Jesus, and keep me there. Let me stop looking elsewhere for life. Let me stay where my sin is exposed, my pride is broken, my guilt is answered, and my only hope is Christ crucified for me.
theological_themes: Renouncing sinful desires and disordered appetites
The inability of idols to heal guilt, sustain weakness, or face death
The cross as the only ground of forgiveness, humility, and hope

scripture_references.connection: This verse speaks of Christ’s blood purifying the conscience, directly supporting the prayer’s claim that only the cross can heal guilt at its deepest level.
Peter connects Christ’s bearing of sin on the cross with believers dying to sin and living to righteousness, grounding both the prayer’s repentance and its hope in the crucified Christ.
Paul’s boast in the cross and rejection of worldly grounds for confidence reflect the prayer’s final desire to be left at the cross as the only safe place for hope.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language of being “chosen of thee from eternity” and “given to Christ” reflects a strongly Reformed doctrine of election, which is biblically grounded but doctrinally contested among Christians.

The phrase “one that has nothing and is nothing” could be misunderstood as denying human dignity as made in God’s image. The adaptation preserves the humility and lack of saving merit while avoiding the implication that human life has no God-given worth.

The original interprets losses of reputation, wealth, and pleasure as God’s providential affliction used by grace. This is a biblical theme, but it requires pastoral care because not every suffering should be simplistically explained as a direct correction for a specific idol.

The requests about the eye, ear, appetite, and lustful heart could be misread as hostility toward the body or ordinary desires. The adaptation frames them as disordered and sinful uses of good faculties, not as a rejection of embodied life itself.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “a shell full of dust” as bodily frailty and creatureliness rather than worthlessness, while retaining the contrast between human weakness and God’s life-giving grace.
I interpreted “vanity of creatures” as the inability of created things to function as ultimate sources of life, joy, or security, not as a denial that creation is good.
I kept the repeated self-rule structure of the original but expressed it in contemporary terms like grabbing the steering wheel, scrambling to secure everything, and editing God’s commands.
I treated “my own Christ” and “my own Spirit” as attempts to save, restore, teach, guide, and govern oneself apart from Christ and the Holy Spirit.
I preserved the stark final movement to the cross as the prayer’s intended resting place, not merely as one devotional image among others.
